pages.c07-p01: Explain how evaluation is used to ensure that a solution: meets the original design criteria; is a full and complete solution; is an efficient solution; and is a robust solution
pages.c07-p02: Explain how evaluation is used to ensure that a solution: meets the original design criteria; is a full and complete solution; is an efficient solution; and is a robust solution

q.q: What does evaluation of a solution mean?
o: Describing what each part of the program does, screen by screen
Judging how well the solution solves the original problem, backed by evidence
Testing each function of the program with valid, invalid and extreme data
Writing the user requirements with the client before the design begins
q.why: Evaluation is a verdict backed by evidence, not a description of the program.

q.q: What is a solution judged against during evaluation?
o: The original user requirements and design criteria
Other programs on the market that do a similar job
The number of lines of code in the finished program
The programmer's own opinion of the finished program
q.why: Requirements are the agreed standard.

q.q: When does evaluation happen?
o: Only at the end, once the program has been released
Only at the start, before any design work is done
Only when a user reports a problem with the program
During development, to refine each version, and at the end
q.why: Evaluation refines each version and decides at the end whether the solution is finished.

q.q: What are user requirements?
o: The hardware and software the system will need in order to run properly
The tests that will be carried out on the finished system by the users
A description of the screens and algorithms that make up the design
The agreed list of what the system must do, written at the start with the client
q.why: User requirements are agreed with the client at the start.

q.q: What are design criteria (success criteria)?
o: The list of features that the client has agreed will not be included in the system
The screen layouts, algorithms and data structures that were planned in the design
Measurable targets taken from the requirements, such as 'a booking can be made in under one minute'
The opinions of users that are collected after the system has been released
q.why: Design criteria are measurable targets taken from the requirements.

q.q: Which is the best example of a measurable design criterion?
o: The booking system should be good
Users should like the booking system
The system should be modern
A booking can be made in under one minute
q.why: A criterion must be measurable so it can be checked with evidence.

q.q: Apart from the requirements and design criteria, what else is the solution measured against?
o: The finished solutions produced by other pupils or developers for the same task
The original design: screen layouts, algorithms and data structures that were planned
The official documentation and help pages for the programming language used
The total number of hours that the programmer spent writing and testing the program
q.why: The original design is also used as a measure.

q.q: What does a functional requirement describe?
o: How well or in what way the system must work
What the system must do
Which devices the system will run on
Who the stakeholders are
q.why: Functional requirements are the things the system must do, such as calculating a hire cost.

q.q: What does a non-functional requirement describe?
o: What the system must do
The list of tests in the test plan
How well or in what way the system must work
The algorithms used in the program
q.why: Non-functional requirements cover qualities such as speed, ease of use and platform.

q.q: Which is a non-functional requirement?
o: Print an invoice for each member
Show search results within one second
Search for a coach by surname
Calculate the monthly fee
q.why: Response time describes how well the system works; the others are things it must do.

q.q: Which is a functional requirement for a kayak hire system?
o: Calculate the hire cost from the number of hours
Respond within 2 seconds of a button being pressed
Be usable by staff after 10 minutes' training
Run on the club's tablets
q.why: Calculating a cost is something the system must do; the others are non-functional.

q.q: Which is a non-functional requirement for a kayak hire system?
o: Print a monthly report of bookings
Search for a customer by name
Store each booking in a file
Usable by staff after 10 minutes' training
q.why: Ease of learning describes how well it works.

q.q: How are functional requirements usually evaluated?
o: By measuring response times with a stopwatch
By testing each function against the test plan
By checking the system runs on the right devices
By asking users which colours they prefer
q.why: Functional requirements are checked function by function using the test plan.

q.q: How might a non-functional requirement such as "usable without training" be evaluated?
o: By observing users trying the system and collecting their feedback
By running the test plan's valid data tests only
By counting the number of lines of code
By checking that the program compiles without errors
q.why: Non-functional requirements are judged by measuring, observing users and checking platforms.

q.q: In evaluation, what does the platform refer to?
o: The devices and operating system the client uses
The programming language the system was written in
The IDE used to develop the program
The number of users who will use the system
q.why: A full evaluation checks the solution runs properly on the intended platform.

q.q: A kayak club requires the system to run on its tablets. Which kind of requirement is this?
o: Non-functional
Functional
Design data requirement
Validation rule
q.why: Running on particular devices is about the platform, a non-functional requirement.

q.q: Which is evidence for an evaluation?
o: The name of the programmer who wrote it
A screenshot of the code editor
The size of the program file
Test plan results and user feedback
q.why: Evaluation needs evidence of how well requirements are met.

q.q: Who are the stakeholders whose feedback is used in an evaluation?
o: Only the programmer who wrote the code
Only the company's shareholders
The client, end users and developers
Only the examiner or moderator
q.why: Stakeholders include the client, the end users and the developers.

q.q: Which method of collecting stakeholder feedback is mentioned in the notes?
o: Reading the program's source code
Compiling the program in a different IDE
Counting the number of variables used
Watching users try the system
q.why: Feedback comes from questionnaires, interviews or watching users try the system.

q.q: Which piece of evidence compares what should happen with what did happen?
o: Test plan results: actual outcomes compared with expected outcomes
Stakeholder feedback collected from a questionnaire after use
The number of steps it takes a user to complete each task
The original list of user requirements agreed with the client
q.why: Test plan results compare actual with expected outcomes.

q.q: When evaluating each requirement, which three judgements can be made?
o: Fully met, partly met or not met
Passed, failed or not tested
Valid, invalid or extreme
Functional, non-functional or optional
q.why: For each requirement decide fully, partly or not met, and point to the evidence.

q.q: When is a solution full and complete?
o: When it has been compiled without syntax errors
When every requirement has been implemented and works
When it has been used by the client for a month
When every function has been unit tested once
q.why: Completeness means all required features are present and working.

q.q: An evaluation finds that a required feature is missing. What should happen?
o: It is ignored, as the rest of the solution works
The requirement is deleted so that the solution is complete
It is recorded as a further improvement, as the requirements show exactly what must be added
The test plan is changed so the feature is no longer tested
q.why: Missing features become improvements; the requirements show the gap.

q.q: How do the user requirements help when a feature is missing?
o: They are the agreed standard, so comparing against them reveals the gap and shows what to add
They contain the code for every feature, so it can be copied in
They list the names of the users who will test the feature
They give the test data that should be used for the feature
q.why: Explain that the requirements are the agreed standard, not just what they contain.

q.q: In the kayak hire evaluation, "Email a receipt to the customer" was not implemented. How should it be recorded?
o: Partly met; the receipt can be printed instead
Fully met; the other features work
Not met; add in the next version
Not met; remove it from the requirements
q.why: A requirement not implemented is not met and becomes an improvement.

q.q: In the kayak hire evaluation, 2 of 3 staff needed help finding the cancel option. How was "Staff can use it without training" judged?
o: Fully met
Not met
Partly met
Not tested
q.why: Some staff managed but two needed help, so it is partly met, with an improvement suggested.

q.q: In the kayak hire evaluation, which improvement was suggested for the cancel option?
o: Remove the cancel option completely
Add a training course for staff
Add a date filter to the report
Move Cancel onto the main menu
q.why: Moving Cancel to the main menu responds to the feedback that staff could not find it.

q.q: In the kayak hire evaluation, what evidence showed the cost calculation was fully met?
o: Staff said that the costs looked about right to them
Tests 1–6 gave the expected costs for 2, 3, 5 and 6 hours
The program compiled first time without any errors
The code for the calculation was only a few lines long
q.why: Test results matching expected outcomes are the evidence.

q.q: Which statement would earn the most credit in an evaluation?
o: The program has a menu with four different options on it
The menu works well and it looks good on the screen
I am pleased with how my menu turned out in the end
Requirement 3 is fully met – all four menu options worked in tests 4–7
q.why: Be evaluative, not descriptive: give a judgement and point to evidence.

q.q: Why does "The program has a menu" earn little credit in an evaluation?
o: It is too short, as each point in an evaluation must be at least a paragraph
It describes the program instead of judging it against a requirement with evidence
Menus are not normally part of the user requirements, so they are not evaluated
It should refer to 'the system' rather than 'the program' to gain the mark
q.why: Evaluation is a verdict backed by evidence, not a description.

q.q: A pupil's evaluation says: "My program is excellent and does everything." What is the main weakness?
o: There is no evidence and no link to individual requirements
It does not describe how the code was written
It does not mention the programming language used
It is written in the first person
q.why: Each judgement should refer to a requirement and point to evidence.

q.q: A requirement says "Print a monthly report of all bookings." Testing shows the report prints but leaves out cancelled bookings, which the client wanted included. How should this be judged?
o: Fully met
Not met
Not a requirement
Partly met
q.why: The feature works in part but does not do everything required.

q.q: Why are design criteria written in a measurable form?
o: So the programmer can write the code more quickly
So the system will run faster on the client's computers
So it can be shown clearly, with evidence, whether each one has been met
So that fewer tests need to be carried out
q.why: Measurable targets can be checked against evidence.

q.q: Which evidence would best show that a booking can be made in under one minute?
o: Reading through the booking code line by line
Checking the booking screen has a title
Asking the programmer whether it is fast
Timing several users as they make a booking
q.why: Measurements such as timings are evidence for a non-functional criterion.

q.q: What is the difference between evaluation and testing?
o: Testing judges the solution against the requirements; evaluation finds syntax errors
Testing checks whether each part works; evaluation judges how well the whole solution meets the requirements using that evidence
Testing is done by users; evaluation is done only by the compiler
There is no difference; the two words mean the same thing
q.why: Test results are one source of evidence for the evaluation.

q.q: A club asked for a system to record bookings and email receipts. The finished system records bookings correctly. Is it a full and complete solution?
o: Yes, because the booking feature passed all its tests
Yes, because it compiles and runs without crashing
No, because emailing receipts has not been implemented
No, because it has not yet been used for a full season
q.why: Every requirement must be implemented and working.

q.q: Why is stakeholder feedback useful in an evaluation?
o: It shows whether the people who use the system find it meets their needs
It replaces the need to write and carry out a test plan
It finds any syntax errors that the compiler has missed
It decides which programming language the system should use
q.why: Users and the client can judge things testing alone cannot, such as ease of use.

q.q: Which is the best example of an improvement linked to evidence?
o: Add a date filter, as staff said finding last month's bookings took too long
Add more colours to the screens to make the program look better
Rewrite the whole program again using a different programming language
Make the program better and easier to use in the next version
q.why: An improvement should be specific and linked to evidence from the evaluation.

q.q: Which question is most useful when evaluating whether a solution meets the original design criteria?
o: Does each requirement have evidence showing it is fully, partly or not met?
How many lines of code does the solution contain?
How long did it take the programmer to write?
Which IDE was used to write the solution?
q.why: Evaluation works through the requirements as a checklist with evidence.

q.q: A school library system must let staff search for a book by title. Which kind of requirement is this?
o: Non-functional
Platform
Robustness
Functional
q.why: Searching is something the system must do.

q.q: A school library system must show search results within two seconds. Which kind of requirement is this?
o: Functional
Non-functional
Validation
Completeness
q.why: Speed describes how well the system works.

q.q: Which is the best way to structure an evaluation of whether the design criteria are met?
o: Work through the requirements as a checklist, judging each with evidence
Describe each screen of the program in the order it appears
List every variable and its data type
Explain how each line of the code works
q.why: Use the requirements as a checklist: fully, partly or not met, with evidence.

q.q: A requirement reads "Store every booking in a file for monthly reports." Tests show bookings are appended and read back correctly. How should it be judged?
o: Fully met
Partly met
Not met
Not testable
q.why: The test evidence shows the requirement works as stated.

q.q: Which of these is an example of a stakeholder?
o: An end user of the system
The compiler
The test plan
The source code
q.why: Stakeholders are people: the client, end users and developers.

q.q: Which is a measurement that could be used as evidence in an evaluation?
o: The programmer's favourite feature
The name of the IDE used
The colour of the main menu
The number of steps a task takes
q.why: Measurements such as response times or steps per task are evidence.

q.q: During development, how is evaluation used?
o: To refine each version before the next is built
To write the original user requirements
To decide which programming language to learn
To replace testing of each module
q.why: Evaluation during development helps refine each version.

q.q: A system meets all its functional requirements but is too slow for staff to use at busy times. Is it fully successful?
o: Yes, because every function works correctly
Yes, because speed is never part of the requirements
No, because it has a syntax error
No, because a non-functional requirement is not met
q.why: A full evaluation judges non-functional requirements as well as functional ones.

q.q: What makes an evaluation "evaluative" rather than "descriptive"?
o: It explains in detail what each screen looks like
It gives a judgement about each requirement backed by evidence
It lists every feature the program contains
It describes how the program was coded
q.why: Evaluation is a verdict backed by evidence.

q.q: Which is the best source of evidence that a requirement for ease of use is met?
o: The program compiling without errors
Observing users complete tasks without help
The number of lines in the source code
A list of the variables used
q.why: Ease of use is shown by watching users and collecting their feedback.

q.q: What is an efficient solution?
o: One that keeps working when given invalid or unexpected data
One that has every requirement implemented and working
One that does its job quickly without wasting resources or the user's time and effort
One that has been tested with valid, extreme and invalid data
q.why: Efficiency covers processor time, memory, storage and the user's effort.

q.q: What is a robust solution?
o: One that keeps working correctly when things go wrong, without crashing or producing wrong results
One that runs quickly and uses little memory or storage
One that has every feature the client asked for
One that is easy for new users to learn
q.why: Robustness means coping with invalid, unexpected and large volumes of data.

q.q: Which describes a robust solution?
o: It was written quickly by an experienced programmer
It uses as few lines of code as it possibly can
It has a colourful and attractive user interface
It copes with invalid and unexpected data without crashing
q.why: Robustness is about handling errors and unexpected input.

q.q: Which change makes a program more efficient?
o: Replacing seven separate variables and additions with an array and a loop
Adding more screens that the user must pass through before each task
Removing the validation checks from all of the inputs to save time
Copying the same block of code into five places where it is needed
q.why: Arrays and loops avoid repetition and scale to any amount of data.

q.q: Which test is designed to check robustness?
o: Entering large volumes of valid, invalid and unexpected data
Entering one typical value and checking the result
Reading through the code line by line
Asking the client which colours they prefer
q.why: Robustness testing uses large volumes and bad data.

q.q: A program accepts letters in a number field and then crashes. What does this show?
o: It is not efficient
It is not robust
It has a syntax error
It is complete
q.why: Failing on unexpected input means it is not robust.

q.q: Which resources should an efficient solution not waste?
o: Only the processor's time while the program is running
Only the storage space the program takes on the hard drive
Processor time, memory, storage and the user's time and effort
Only the programmer's own time while writing the code
q.why: Efficiency includes the user's effort as well as computer resources.

q.q: A task needs a user to go through three screens when one menu choice would do. Which quality is weak?
o: Robustness
Efficiency
Completeness
Validation
q.why: Making users take extra steps wastes their time and effort.

q.q: Which question helps to evaluate efficiency?
o: Does the program reject letters in a number field?
Does the program still work if the data file is deleted?
Has every requirement been implemented?
Are response times acceptable with a realistic amount of data?
q.why: Response times are evidence of efficiency; the others are robustness and completeness.

q.q: Which feature of code structure makes a solution more efficient?
o: The same calculation copied into each place it is needed
A separate variable for every value instead of an array
A search that always checks every item even after a match
User-defined functions that are reused instead of repeated code
q.why: Reused functions, loops and arrays avoid repetition and unnecessary work.

q.q: A linear search carries on checking every item even after the target has been found. How could it be made more efficient?
o: Add a range check on the target before searching
Add a try … catch block around the search
Stop the search as soon as the item is found, using a found flag
Search the list twice to make sure the target is there
q.why: Stopping once found avoids unnecessary work.

q.q:
int[] cars = { 120, 95, 143, 101, 88, 60, 72 };
Why is a loop over this array more efficient code than int total = mon + tue + wed + thu + fri + sat + sun;?
o: It makes the total larger because more values are added
It removes the need to store the values in memory
It stops the program crashing if a value is missing
It avoids writing out separate variables and additions, and works for any number of days
q.why: One array and a loop scale to any amount of data without repeating code.

q.q:
int[] cars = { 120, 95, 143, 101, 88, 60, 72 };
A loop adds every element to total, starting from 0. What is output?
Which techniques improve the robustness of a program?
o: Loops, arrays and reusable functions
A simpler interface with fewer screens
Validation, error trapping and testing every path
More colours and larger fonts on each screen
q.why: Robustness is improved by validation and error trapping; loops and arrays improve efficiency.

q.q: Which techniques improve the efficiency of a program?
o: Validation, error trapping and testing every path
Presence, length, type and format checks
try … catch blocks around every input
Loops, arrays, functions and a simpler interface
q.why: Efficiency comes from good structure and fewer user steps.

q.q: What is high-volume testing?
o: Testing the program with the loudspeaker volume set to maximum
Testing each module many times in a row with the same value
Testing the program with one very large number
Entering or loading large amounts of data to check the system still performs and does not fail
q.why: High-volume testing checks the system under heavy use.

q.q: Why is testing with only sensible data not enough to show a program is robust?
o: Sensible data cannot be entered into most programs
Sensible data always causes the program to crash
Any program looks fine with sensible data; robustness is shown by how it handles bad data and heavy use
Robustness can only be shown by reading the code
q.why: Robustness is measured by invalid, exceptional and high-volume data.

q.q: Which unexpected action should be tried when testing robustness?
o: Entering a typical value in the middle of the range
Following the instructions exactly as written
Using the system for one short task
Pressing Enter on a blank prompt
q.why: Unexpected actions include blank entries, letters in number fields, very long text and deleting the data file.

q.q: A tester deletes the data file and then starts the program, which shows "No bookings file found – a new one has been created." What does this show?
o: The program is not robust, as it lost the bookings
The program is efficient, as it created a file quickly
The program is robust, as it recovers from a missing file
The program is not complete, as the file was missing
q.why: Coping with a missing file and recovering shows robustness.

q.q: A program is tested by loading 50 000 bookings. It slows down a little but gives the correct results and does not crash. What does this show?
o: It is not robust, because it slowed down slightly
It is not complete, because it took longer than usual
It copes with high volumes of data, which is evidence of robustness
It has a logic error, because the time changed
q.why: High-volume testing that passes without failure is evidence of robustness.

q.q: For "How could robustness be tested?", what should a full answer include?
o: At least two kinds of data, such as invalid and high volumes, and the result that shows it is robust
One kind of data, such as typical values, and a description of the code
A list of the requirements and whether each is met
A description of how fast the program runs
q.why: Refer to two kinds of data and say that bad data is rejected with a message and the program does not crash.

q.q: Which result would show that a program is robust when invalid data is entered?
o: It accepts the data and uses it in the calculation
It rejects the data with a helpful message and does not crash
It stops and shows the exception name to the user
It closes so that the data cannot be stored
q.why: Robust programs reject bad data helpfully and keep running.

q.q: Which evidence would best support a judgement about efficiency?
o: Results of invalid, extreme and null data tests
Response times, the number of steps a task takes, and the code structure
The number of crashes during high-volume testing
The list of features that were not implemented
q.why: Those are the efficiency evidence; the second and third are robustness evidence.

q.q: Which evidence would best support a judgement about robustness?
o: Invalid, extreme, null and high-volume test results with no crashes
Response times and the number of steps that a task takes
The total number of lines of code in the finished program
Feedback from users saying that they like the colour scheme
q.why: Robustness is judged from how the system handles bad data and heavy use.

q.q: A program accepts an age of 250 and uses it in a calculation without complaint. Which quality is weak?
o: Efficiency
Completeness
Robustness
Response time
q.why: Accepting impossible data and producing wrong results shows a lack of robustness.

q.q: A search takes 20 seconds to find a member in a list of 300. Which quality is weak?
o: Robustness
Completeness
Efficiency
Validation
q.why: Slow response with a realistic amount of data is an efficiency problem.

q.q: A program crashes when a user types a very long name of 500 characters. Which quality is weak?
o: Efficiency
Completeness
Robustness
Readability
q.why: Failing on unexpected input is a robustness problem.

q.q: A programmer replaces the same 10-line block, which appears four times, with one function called four times. Which quality is improved?
o: Robustness of the input
Efficiency of the code
Completeness of the requirements
Validation of the data
q.why: Reusing a function instead of repeating code improves efficiency and maintenance.

q.q: A program adds int.TryParse to every number input. Which quality is improved?
o: Efficiency
Completeness
Response time
Robustness
q.why: Type checks stop letters crashing the program.

q.q: Why should error messages be checked when evaluating robustness?
o: Error messages slow the program down, so they should be removed
The user should understand what went wrong and be able to recover
Error messages show that the program is complete
Error messages are needed for high-volume testing to work
q.why: A robust system gives helpful messages and lets the user recover.

q.q: A program is fast and uses little memory but crashes whenever a field is left blank. Which statement is correct?
o: It is robust but not efficient
It is both efficient and robust
It is efficient but not robust
It is neither efficient nor complete
q.why: Speed and low memory show efficiency; crashing on blank input shows it is not robust.

q.q: A program never crashes, whatever is typed, but makes users fill in the same details on three separate screens. Which statement is correct?
o: It is robust but not efficient
It is efficient but not robust
It is complete but not robust
It is neither robust nor efficient
q.why: Coping with any input is robustness; repeating details wastes user effort.

q.q: Which question asks about robustness rather than efficiency?
o: Does it keep working with bad, unexpected or large amounts of data?
Does it work without wasting time, resources or effort?
Can users complete tasks in few steps?
Is the code structured with loops and functions?
q.why: Robustness is about coping with bad or large amounts of data.

q.q: Which is the best evaluative statement about robustness?
o: The program is robust because I wrote it carefully
The program is robust: tests 8–12 entered letters, blanks and out-of-range values and each was rejected with a message
The program has validation on some of the inputs
The program should be robust, as it uses C#
q.why: A good evaluation gives a judgement backed by specific test evidence.

q.q: How does validation help to make a solution robust?
o: It makes the program run faster by skipping unnecessary steps
It adds missing features so the solution is complete
It reduces the amount of memory the program needs
It rejects invalid input before it can cause wrong results or crashes
q.why: Validation stops bad data getting in.

q.q: How does error trapping help to make a solution robust?
o: It makes every calculation in the program run in fewer steps
It checks that every one of the requirements has been implemented
It reduces the number of screens that the user must go through
It catches run-time errors such as a missing file so the program does not crash
q.why: try … catch lets the program recover instead of crashing.

q.q: A system for a busy sports centre will be used by many staff at once with thousands of records. Which test is most important to check it will not fail in real use?
o: Testing a single booking with typical data
High-volume testing with realistic amounts of data
Checking the program compiles without errors
Reading the code to check variable names
q.why: High-volume testing checks the system performs under realistic heavy use.

q.q: A programmer says the program is efficient because it was "quick to write". Why is this not a valid judgement?
o: Efficiency is about how the solution runs and the effort it saves users, not how long it took to write
Efficiency is only about how much storage the program uses
Programs that are quick to write are always robust instead
Efficiency can only be judged by the client, not the programmer
q.why: An efficient solution runs quickly without wasting resources or user effort.

q.q: Which pair of tests gives evidence of both efficiency and robustness?
o: Entering one typical value, and reading the code
Timing a search on 10 000 records, and entering letters in a number field
Checking the program compiles, and checking its file size
Asking users their favourite colour, and counting variables
q.why: Timing gives efficiency evidence; bad input gives robustness evidence.

q.q: Which statement about efficiency and robustness is correct?
o: Both are judged only from the programmer's opinion
Both should be judged with evidence from testing
Efficiency is judged by testing, but robustness is not
Robustness is judged by testing, but efficiency is not
q.why: Both efficiency and robustness are judged with evidence from testing.

q.q: Which word describes a program that copes with unexpected input without failing?
o: Efficient
Complete
Functional
Robust
q.why: Robustness is coping with bad or unexpected input.

q.q: Which word describes a program that does its job quickly without wasting resources?
o: Efficient
Robust
Complete
Validated
q.why: Efficiency is about speed and not wasting resources or effort.

q.q: A program stores 30 pupil marks in 30 separate variables. Which change would make it more efficient?
o: Add a presence check to each variable
Put each variable in a try block
Use one array and a loop
Add a second set of 30 variables
q.why: An array with a loop avoids repeated code and scales to any number of marks.

q.q: Which test result would show a lack of robustness?
o: The program rejects a blank entry with a message
The program accepts a valid booking of 3 hours
The program crashes when Enter is pressed on a blank prompt
The program takes one second to show results
q.why: Crashing on blank input means it is not robust.

q.q: A program shows "Please enter a number from 1 to 8" when 12 is typed, then asks again. What does this show?
o: It is not robust, as 12 was rejected
It is robust for out-of-range input
It is efficient, as it responded quickly
It is incomplete, as 12 was not stored
q.why: Rejecting bad data with a helpful message and letting the user recover shows robustness.

q.q: Which is an example of the program wasting the user's effort?
o: Rejecting an invalid date with a helpful message
Using a drop-down list for the pitch size
Showing the total cost clearly at the end
Making the user type their name again on every screen
q.why: Repeating input wastes the user's time and effort, reducing efficiency.

q.q: Which of these improves efficiency rather than robustness?
o: Adding a range check on the number of nights
Catching FileNotFoundException with try … catch
Stopping a search as soon as the item is found
Testing with invalid and null data
q.why: Avoiding unnecessary work improves efficiency; the others improve or test robustness.

q.q: Which of these improves robustness rather than efficiency?
o: Replacing repeated code with a function
Adding a type check on a number input
Reducing the number of screens in a task
Using an array instead of many variables
q.why: A type check stops bad input crashing the program.

q.q: A program works correctly for 10 records but crashes when 10 000 are loaded. Which test found this?
o: Unit testing with typical data
A dry run with a trace table
High-volume testing
A presence check on the input
q.why: Loading large amounts of data is high-volume testing.

q.q: Which evidence shows a program is efficient for users?
o: The program rejects letters in a number field
The program still works with the data file deleted
Users can complete a booking in two steps
The program accepts the extreme value 14
q.why: Few steps per task shows efficiency for the user.

q.q: Which statement about a robust solution is true?
o: It produces results quickly, whatever the data
It contains every feature listed in the requirements
It neither crashes nor produces wrong results when given bad data
It can only be achieved with very short code
q.why: A robust solution rejects bad data instead of crashing or giving wrong results.
